original_question: Which surgical procedure commonly performed to treat chronic tonsillitis and obstructive sleep apnea may cause dysgeusia?

final_qi.question: Which surgical procedure commonly performed to treat chronic tonsillitis and obstructive sleep apnea may cause dysgeusia?
final_qi.search_keyword: surgical procedure chronic tonsillitis obstructive sleep apnea dysgeusia
final_qi.long_answer: Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty (UPPP) is a surgery frequently performed to treat both chronic tonsillitis and obstructive sleep apnea. The procedure involves removal or remodeling of tissues in the throat such as the soft palate, uvula, and tonsils, with the aim of widening the airway to prevent blockages during sleep. A known complication of UPPP is dysgeusia, which refers to an alteration in taste sensation. This change can occur due to nerve injury or other modifications of the oral structures during the surgical procedure.

- Wikipedia: Information about: Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty
Section: Introduction
Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty (abbreviated as UPPP or UP3) is a type of sleep surgery, which are surgical procedures for sleep-related breathing disorders, especially obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty involves removal and/or remodeling of tissues in the throat in order to prevent obstruction of the airway during sleep. Tissues which may typically be removed include the paryngeal tonsils and the adenoid tonsil. Tissues which may typically be remodeled include the uvula (see uvulotomy), the soft palate, and parts of the pharynx. UPPP is the most common surgical procedure performed for OSA.[1][2]
Section: Background
OSA is one of the most common types of sleep-related breathing disorder. It involves obstruction of the upper airway during sleep. Loud snoring and apnea (periods of no breathing) followed by gasping and choking are signs of the condition. The main treatment is continuous positive airway pressure and a range of other measures such sleeping on the side and mandibular advancement splints.
Section: Definition
UPPP with tonsillectomy / adenoidectomy Laser assisted uvulopalatoplasty (LAUP) Palatal stiffening (pillar procedure) Cautery assisted palatal stiffening operation (CAPSO)
Section: Indications
UPPP may be indicated if all of the following are true: Diagnosis of obstructive sleep apnea Failure of non invasive treatments (e.g., continuous positive airway pressure, mandibular advancement splint) Site of airway obstruction identified (soft palate) and amenable to correction with UPPP Too little space (craniofacial anomaly) Too much tissue (tissue hypertrophy or obesity) Tissue too lax (nerve damage, poor muscle tone)
Section: Contraindications
Morbid obesity / Body mass index more than 40kg/m2.[1] Retrognathia (small lower jaw).[3] Retroglossia (tongue positioned further back than normal).[3] Narrowing of the hypopharynx (laryngopharynx).[3] Success rate is only 5% when hypopharyneal narrowing is present.[2] If combined with maxillomandibular advancement, UPPP may still be possible.[2] Sagittal (front-to-back) orientation of airway.[3]
Section: Technique
First, the surgeon cuts into the soft palate starting from a point above the palatal tonsil towards the uvula. Then, the mucosa of the soft palate, tonsillar fossa, and side of the uvula is separated from the underlying tissue layers and removed, leaving any excess nasal mucosa. The edges of the remaining mucosa are sutured back together and the tonsillar pillars may be sutured closed. If the uvula is long, it is shortened or removed completely. Often, the palatal tonsils are removed at the same time, if they have not already been removed. The result of UPPP is that the soft palate is shortened by removing a wedge of excess mucosa from the palate. UPPP decreases the amount of anterior-posterior (front to back) palatal collapse and widens the pharyngeal airway.[1] UPPP may be combined with other types of sleep surgery to address airway obstruction at different sites. This is termed the multilevel surgery. The effectiveness of UPPP is increased when it is combined with another procedure as a multilevel surgery. Examples include UPPP with tonsillectomy or UPPP with a hypopharyngeal procedure such as tongue base reduction or hyoid suspension or UPPP with radiofrequency ablation.[1]
Section: Modifications of uvulopalatopharyngoplasty
Powell’s uvulopalatal flap (introduced in 1996).[7] Extended uvulopalatal flap (EUPF; 2003).[7] Lateral pharyngoplasty (LP; 2003).[7] Expansion sphincter pharyngoplasty (ESP; 2007).[7] Microdebrider-assisted extended uvulopalatoplasty (MEUP; 2008).[7] Relocation pharyngoplasty (rPP; 2009).[7] Soft palate webbing flap (SPWF; 2015).[7]
Section: Complications
Negative-pressure pulmonary edema (post-obstructive pulmonary edema).[1] Bleeding (1-2% risk, which may occur at any time in the first 2 weeks after the procedure).[1] Persistent pain (more than 2 weeks after the procedure).[1] Upper airway edema may be too much when UPPP is done at the same time as maxillomandibular advancement.[2]
Possible long-term complications: Dysphagia (possibly related to undiagnosed gastroesophageal reflux disease).[1] Dysgeusia (change in sense of taste).[1] Globus pharyngis (a sensation of something being stuck in the throat; in up to 31% of cases).[1] Xerostomia (dry mouth) and dry throat, which may be related to loss of the uvula.[6]
